title: When to Rip the Band-Aid Off and Make the Damn Decision
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This Admired Leadership Field Note argues that leaders almost always carry a short list of problems they know they should address but have not, and that research points toward deciding sooner. It offers four conditions under which a leader should stop waiting: the problem will grow while they wait, it sits with one person but now affects others, the bad news will surface whether or not the leader acts, or the leader already knows enough to decide but is stalled by complexity. For each condition it explains the cost of delay, such as multiplying patches, spreading harm, and lost control over timing, framing, and trust. The piece concludes that if any one of the four conditions is true, waiting is no longer prudence but avoidance, and that the discomfort of acting passes faster than the cost of not acting.
points: Problems rarely improve with age; a problem spawning additional problems must be dealt with decisively.
When one person's problem is now costing others, delay shifts the price onto people who did not create it.
Leaders who tell inevitable bad news themselves keep control of timing, framing, and response, and protect trust.
Complexity is often used as cover for discomfort; if the right answer is known, waiting for clarity is avoidance.
The four conditions give a quick test to run against the list of problems a leader has been putting off.
quotes: Problems rarely age well. Unlike wine, they commonly sour with age.
Problems that grow tend to get patched rather than fixed, but the patches multiply until something breaks. Leaders who wait allow the problem to compound, causing more harm than necessary.

Once the cost spreads beyond an individual, the leader confronts a multilayered problem with tentacles that can spread even further without predictability. When others are paying the price for the leader’s delay, it is time to act.
Leaders who get ahead of bad news control the timing, the framing, and the response. Leaders who wait lose all three, and often trust along with them.
Leaders who refuse to decide until the complexity magically fades away are usually delaying because they are uncomfortable, not because the decision isn’t straightforward.
Leaders rarely look back on a hard call and wish they had waited longer. More often, they wish they had acted much sooner.
If the problem is growing, spreading to others, about to surface on its own, or already clear enough to decide, waiting is no longer prudence. It is avoidance.
